name: Proto-Kayan
notes: Long Naah, Data Dian, Balui Liko, Busang and Bahau (Smith 2017a: 52-62). Smith calls the phonological evidence for Kayan 'relatively weak' (p. 60) and rests the group on lexical innovations (pp. 60-62). Figure 10 (p. 54) lists the PMP to Proto-Kayan changes. Glottolog's Kayanic (kaya1333) is this group (Kayan languages and Bahau). Proto-Kayanic (Smith's Table 23, p. 86) and Proto-Kayan-Murik-Merap (section 2.2.4.1) are held back as intermediate stages; their changes are entered on this node (decision kayanic-held).

name: Proto-Murik-Merap
notes: Ngorek (Murik) and Merap (Smith 2017a: 62-72; Smith 2017b). Smith calls Merap 'an aberrant dialect of Ngorek' (2017a: 67), and Glottolog's Murik (muri1259), a language, has Ngorek, Pua', Merap and Huang Bau as dialects; the node is entered as Smith names it. Proto-Kayanic (Smith's Table 23, p. 86) and Proto-Kayan-Murik-Merap (section 2.2.4.1) are held back as intermediate stages; their changes are entered on this node (decision kayanic-held).

name: Proto-Segai-Modang

name: Proto-Kajang
notes: Sekapan, Kejaman and Lahanan (Smith 2017a: 93-99; Figure 23, p. 97). The fricative *ɮ from *l in the onset of the final syllable is 'unique in all of Borneo' (p. 95). The internal subgrouping is unresolved (pp. 96-97). Smith finds no evidence for a Melanau-Kajang node (pp. 106-111, Figure 26), so Kajang and Melanau are entered separately under PMP. Figure 23 also has *CC > *ʔC (clusters from the loss of a middle vowel in three-syllable words, p. 96), not entered as a row. Glottolog's Kajang (kaja1255) has the same members.

name: Proto-Melanau

Smith thinks it 'likely' that final high vowels had become *əw and *əy in Proto-Melanau (p. 103); nothing else is assigned to it. Glottolog's Melanau (mela1255) has the same members.

name: Proto-Punan
notes: Punan Tubu, Punan Bah, Punan Aput, Beketan, Ukit and others (Smith 2017a: 111-127; Figure 27, p. 112). 'Proto-Punan had not undergone any major changes'; the subgroup rests on lexical innovations, above all the metathesis *təlaʔus > *təlasuʔ 'barking deer' (p. 114). Smith treats Punan as one language with dialects (p. 120). His internal split into Punan Tubu-Bah and the rest (Figures 28-29, pp. 122-124) has conflicting evidence (p. 122), so no lower nodes are entered; the changes are entered on each lect. Table 31 has '?' for PMP *r. Glottolog's Punan (puna1280) follows Smith's grouping.
inherit_note: Unchanged from PMP in Table 31 (p. 114), which sets PMP and Proto-Punan side by side.

name: Proto-Müller-Schwaner
notes: Aoheng, Seputan, Hovongan and Kereho (Smith 2017a: 127-139; Figure 30). Table 39 and Figure 31 (pp. 128-129) give the reconstruction. Smith keeps it apart from Punan here and discusses a Punan-Müller-Schwaner link in chapter 3 (pp. 330-335), which is not entered. His internal subgrouping has three primary branches (Upper Mahakam, Kereho, Hovongan; Figure 38, p. 139), so no lower nodes are entered. Table 39 has '?' for PMP *r. Glottolog's Muller-Schwaner (mull1247) has the same members.
inherit_note: Unchanged from PMP in Table 39 (p. 128), which sets PMP and Proto-Müller-Schwaner side by side.

name: Proto-Land Dayak
notes: Smith 2017a, section 2.6 (pp. 139-167). 'The most prominent sound change with subgrouping value' is *R > *h and *l > *r (p. 142), but it is not attested in every language (Hliboi and Sungkung have l), so the subgroup rests mainly on lexical innovations (pp. 143-149). Many words are Malayic loans, and some reflexes could not be identified (p. 140). Smith's internal subgrouping (Figure 45, p. 193) differs from an earlier classification by Rensch and colleagues. Glottolog's Land Dayak (land1261) follows Smith.
